docs.title: Welcome
docs.text: Selena Wang, PhD selewang@iu.edu Department of Biostatistics and Health Data Science HITS 3071 410 W. 10th Street Indianapolis, IN 46202 Dr. Wang is a tenure-track Assistant Professor in the Department of Biostatistics and Health Data Science at Indiana University School of Medicine. She has an interdisciplinary background in biostatistics and computational psychology, with expertise in developing statistical and computational methods for complex, high-dimensional biomedical and networked data. Her research advances generative embedding, scalable methods and software for high-dimensional networked data, and Bayesian inference for brain and protein networks, with applications in disease subtyping, brain–behavior linkage, biomarker identification, and disease pathway discovery, particularly in Alzheimer's disease and other psychiatric and psychological conditions. Her work has been published in leading journals, including Nature Methods, Alzheimer's & Dementia, Medical Image Analysis, Psychometrika, Psychological Methods, and Human Brain Mapping. Dr. Wang has been named a William H. Gates Sr. Fellow by Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative, a Research Career Institute in the Mental Health of Aging (CIMA) Scholar and a Research Education Component (REC) Scholar of the Indiana Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. Her methodological research program is supported by the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative and the National Institute on Aging.

docs.title: Postdoctoral Fellow
docs.text: Dr. Jaeyoung Lee                      Dr. Jaeyoung Lee is a postdoctoral fellow in the lab. He received his doctoral training in Statistics at Virginia Tech, where his dissertation focused on supervised variational autoencoder frameworks for predictive modeling and association analysis. His research interests include heterogeneous data learning, deep generative models, variational inference, Bayesian methods, latent space models, dimension reduction, and statistical machine learning. In the lab, he develops statistical and machine learning methods for high-dimensional biomedical and neuroimaging data.

docs.title: Ph.D. Students
docs.text: Renhao Li                      Renhao Li is a Ph.D. student working with our team. His research focuses on statistical and computational methods for high-dimensional biomedical data, with interests in network modeling, machine learning, and neuroimaging applications.                  Luling Altan                      Luling Altan is a Ph.D. student in SWLab. Her research focuses on developing Bayesian methodology for complex networks, particularly brain and protein networks. She suspects that much of what we observe is a projection from a much higher-dimensional space, and that the most interesting part of a dataset often lies in its latent structure rather than the features we directly measure. With a background in mathematics, she is drawn to graph theory and its applications in neuroscience for this reason. In her spare time, she loves rock climbing, researching the art of raising cats, reading about Vedic astrology, photographing nebulae and galaxies, and predicting people's destinies with star charts.                  Presentations: ENAR 2026 Spring Meeting poster: Bayesian latent space co-evolution model to explain AD progression ·                     SMI 2026: Alzheimer's Disease Subtype Identification from Spatial Tau-PET Heterogeneity Using Self-Supervised Deep Learning ·                     20th International Joint Conference on Computational and Financial Econometrics (IJCFE, December 2026)

docs.text: Ash Sharma Ash Sharma has a background in computer science and statistics. His research focuses on statistical and machine learning methods for high-dimensional neuroimaging and biological data, including latent-variable approaches to neuroimaging reliability and proteomic signatures of brain microstructural integrity.                                       He presented the first-author poster Proteomics signature of whole-brain microstructural integrity of white matter using LatentSNA at the 2026 Alzheimer's Association International Conference (AAIC). He also contributed code fixes to the LatentSNA package, including ensuring the Sutheta prior is positive-definite, proper initialization before the MCMC loop, and error handling.                  Bilal Sultan                      Bilal Sultan is a research assistant working with our team. Rahul Bathala                      Rahul Bathala is a research assistant working with our team. docs.title: Research
docs.text:
Network science is interdisciplinary. Focusing on improving current analytical strategies, we absorb influences of other disciplines to inform and improve understandings about human behaviors with applications in neuroscience, psychiatry, psychology, and others. Broadly speaking, we model real-world networks with statistically sound principles and methods—reduce network complexity, perform intuitive visualization, and test critical hypotheses with improved statistical power and controlled type I errors. We are particularly interested in the topological structures of networks and the roles they play in (neuro)degeneration, (neuro)development, and resilience.

Selected publications by research theme. For the complete list, see the Publications page.

docs.title: JNIRM
docs.text:
Relationships among teachers are known to influence their teaching-related perceptions, and the paper studies whether and how teachers' advising relationships (networks) are related to their perceptions of satisfaction, students, and influence over educational policies, recorded as responses to a questionnaire (item responses). The Joint Network and Item Response Model (JNIRM) is a joint model of network and item responses with correlated latent variables that allows the analyst to test and interpret the dependence between a network and item responses. In the paper, teachers' advising relationships contribute to their perceptions of satisfaction and students more often than their perceptions of influence over educational policies.

The package takes an N × N social network (adjacency) matrix and an N × P item response matrix, and produces joint latent positions for the network and the response items from which the dependence between the two data sources can be tested and interpreted. It includes model fitting, cross-validation, and goodness-of-fit evaluation of both the network and response components.

Code: GitHub Repository

Paper: Wang, S., Sweet, T. M., & Paul, S. (2026). The co-varying ties between networks and item responses via latent variables. Psychometrika, 91(2), 641–668.

docs.title: jlsm
docs.text:
In social, behavioral, and economic sciences, researchers often study a social network among a group of individuals together with high-dimensional attribute measurements, such as questionnaire responses. The joint latent space model (JLSM) summarizes the network and the multivariate attributes in a single person–attribute joint latent space, estimated with a Variational Bayesian EM algorithm. This allows effective integration, informative visualization, and prediction of social networks and attributes. In the paper, JLSM is applied to the French financial elites and reveals a division in their social circles in accordance with differences in career, political views, and social status.

The package takes an N × N social network adjacency matrix and an N × P matrix of multivariate attribute measurements, and produces joint latent positions for persons and attributes from which both data sources can be jointly visualized, estimated, and predicted. It builds on lvm4net and supports posterior sampling, visualization, and prediction workflows.

Code: GitHub Repository

Paper: Wang, S., Paul, S., & De Boeck, P. (2023). Joint latent space model for social networks with multivariate attributes. Psychometrika, 88(4), 1197–1227.

docs.title: ABCModel
docs.text:
Group-level brain structural connectivity is commonly summarized by entry-wise sample means or medians across individual connectivity matrices, which ignores the associations among structural connections and the topological properties of brain networks. The Attributes-informed Brain Connectivity (ABC) model is a latent space-based generative network model that offers an interpretable latent space representation of the group-level connectivity, incorporates the anatomical knowledge of nodes and tests its co-varying relationship with connectivity, and quantifies the uncertainty of the estimated group-level effects. A novel Bayesian MCMC algorithm estimates the model, and in the paper it identifies meaningful sex-specific network neuromarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

The package takes a list of V × V brain connectivity matrices (X) and a list of V × P region-level attribute matrices (Y), along with covariate matrices for the connectivity (W) and attribute (H) data, and produces a group-level estimate of connectivity informed by the attributes, with a tunable latent dimension K for the multiplicative attribute effects. Simulated example data and code are included.

Code: GitHub Repository

Paper: Wang, S., Wang, Y., Xu, F. H., Shen, L., Zhao, Y., & Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. (2025). Establishing group-level brain structural connectivity incorporating anatomical knowledge under latent space modeling. Medical Image Analysis, 99, 103309.

Tutorial: ABC Model Tutorial

Simulation Example: Example Files

docs.title: LatentSNA
docs.text:
LatentSNA addresses the lack of statistical power and inflated type II errors in current analytic approaches for detecting imaging biomarkers. It implements network science in a generative Bayesian framework that preserves neurologically meaningful brain topology, improving statistical power for imaging biomarker detection. It enables unbiased estimation of the influence of biomarkers on behavioral variants, quantifies the uncertainty of those effects and evaluates their likelihood against chance, and improves brain–behavior prediction in new samples across multiple imaging modalities and outcome measures.

The package takes a list of V × V brain connectivity matrices (X) and an N × P outcome matrix (Y). It estimates the latent variable values for each participant that characterize their individual connectivity, estimates the covariances between the connectome and the behaviors with 95% credible intervals, tests whether the connectivity of a brain region is related to the behaviors, and predicts both connectivity and behavior in new samples. Simulated example data—a list of V × V connectivity matrices (X) and an N × P outcome matrix (Y)—are included for demonstration.

Code: GitHub Repository

Paper: Wang, S., Zhang, X., Liu, Y., Xu, W., Tian, X., & Zhao, Y. (2026). Latent space-based network analysis for brain–behavior linking in neuroimaging. Nature Methods, 23(1), 225–235.

Tutorial: LatentSNA Tutorial

docs.title: Prospective Students
docs.text:
(2026) I am looking for motivated students to contribute to complex networks and systems research to investigate biomedical complexity at the SWLab. The SWLab is housed within the department of biostatistics and health data science at IU School of Medicine. The lab focuses on applying and developing scalable statistical and computational approaches for high-dimensional biomedical data with emphases on network science, high dimensional data analysis, neuroimaging, data integration and statistical machine learning. Depending on prior experiences, selected candidates will have the opportunity to contribute to substantive neuroscience research, method innovations or software development and documentation.

If you possess the following qualifications, I strongly encourage you to consider applying:

  1. Have a background or prior experience in neuroimaging, network analysis, or computational neuroscience.
  2. Skilled in programming and/or statistical method development.

If you are interested in joining my lab, please email me the following documents with the subject “Prospective student for SWLab”:

  1. Your CV
  2. A brief description of your background and interest

docs.title: Application Process:
docs.text: Apply to the Department of Biostatistics and Health Data Science at Indiana University School of Medicine. More information here.

docs.title: Current Indiana Students:
docs.text: If you are a current Indiana student interested in working with me, please send me an email with your CV/resume and a brief description of your background and interest. I am interested in students who want to pursue PhD education. Funding availability may vary and cannot be guaranteed for all applicants.
